Chapter 5. Stretching Capabilities Through Challenge: The Challenger Discipline.
Let’s dive into what it really means to act as a Challenger. Imagine someone who never settles for “good enough.” Multipliers—those leaders who truly bring out the best in others—don’t stick with the status quo or take easy answers. Instead, they challenge people to reach further, to go beyond what they think is possible.
What’s at the heart of this discipline? It’s the belief that when you give people the chance and the right support, they’re capable of solving even the toughest problems. Rather than handing out every solution, Challengers ask bold questions. They set ambitious goals, then invite everyone to figure out how to get there together.
So, what does this look like day to day? There are a few key practices that really set Challengers apart.
First, they frame opportunities boldly. Instead of seeing problems as roadblocks, they present them as exciting chances to shine. Picture a leader saying, “How could we double our impact with just half the resources?” That kind of question doesn’t just challenge the team—it sparks curiosity and opens up creative thinking.
Next, Challengers are masters at asking the right questions. Rather than giving orders, they ask open-ended questions that make people stop and really think. These questions stretch assumptions and encourage everyone to think bigger and broader.
Another big one is expressing confidence in others. Challengers show their teams they truly believe in them. And you know what? That kind of faith is contagious. When someone believes in you, it’s a lot easier to believe in yourself—and to take on bigger challenges.
Challengers also focus on encouraging ownership. Instead of stepping in with their own solutions, they invite the team to take responsibility and figure things out. It’s about giving people the space—and the trust—to solve problems their own way.
Let’s put this into a real-world context. Imagine a department head who suddenly faces a big budget cut. Instead of rolling out a strict cost-cutting plan, they gather the team and ask, “What creative ways can we keep delivering value with fewer resources?” The team gets together, brainstorms, tries new ideas—and in the end, finds better ways to work that actually boost performance.
This is so different from what Diminishers do. Sometimes, Diminishers try to protect their teams from tough challenges—or they might overwhelm them with demands, but give no support. Either way, people don’t get the chance to grow or to innovate.
Here’s the key takeaway: The Challenger discipline is all about setting the bar high and trusting people to rise to meet it. It takes courage, patience, and a willingness to let others struggle and learn along the way. But when it’s done well, it leads to real breakthroughs, not just for individuals, but for the whole organization.
